An introduction
Agentic AI
From AI that answers to AI that acts
David Pai · Computer Science, Mendocino College
01 · Definition
What is agentic AI?
An AI system that pursues a goal by planning its own steps, using tools, checking the results and adjusting, with limited human direction.
Chatbot
You decide every step
Answers one prompt at a time. Nothing happens until you ask the next question.
Scripted automation
A programmer decided in advance
Follows fixed steps. Fast and reliable, but breaks when the situation changes.
AI agent
The model decides as it goes
Chooses the next action from what it just learned, until the goal is met.
02 · How it works
The agent loop
Goal
“Find why last night’s backup failed and fix it.”
→
Plan
Break the goal into steps and pick the next one.
→
Act
Call a tool: read a log, run a command, search.
→
Observe
Read the result. Done? If not, plan again.
↺ repeat until the goal is met, or a limit is reached
Model
The reasoning engine (an LLM)
Tools
APIs, code, files, browser, search
Memory
Context, notes and history it carries
Guardrails
Permissions, budgets, human approval
03 · Where it fits
Where agentic AI works best
Software engineering
Write, test and fix code across a whole repository
Research & synthesis
Search many sources, compare them, write a cited report
IT & security operations
Triage alerts, gather evidence, draft a fix or response
Customer support
Resolve tickets end to end using account systems
Back-office workflows
Invoices, onboarding and data entry across several apps
Personal productivity
Email, calendars, documents and scheduling
The common thread: multi-step work, done with digital tools, with results someone can check.
04 · Deciding
Is this task right for an agent?
1
Does the path vary?
The steps depend on what it finds along the way.
2
Can it reach the tools?
Systems and data are available by API, command line or browser.
3
Can success be checked?
Tests, rules or a reviewer can tell right from wrong.
4
Are mistakes recoverable?
Errors are cheap, reversible or caught before they cause harm.
5
Is it worth the cost?
Volume or value justifies the compute, delay and oversight.
Mostly yes
Good agent candidate
Start small, with a human reviewing the output.
Steps never change
Use a script or workflow
Cheaper, faster and fully predictable.
High stakes, no check
Keep a human in charge
Let AI assist, but people decide and act.

06 · Building
How to build an agent
Step 1
Define the job
One task, clear inputs and a measurable definition of done
Step 2
Choose the model
A strong reasoning model for planning; smaller ones for routine steps
Step 3
Give it tools
APIs, code execution, search, files; MCP connects them in a standard way
Step 4
Write instructions
Role, rules, examples, and when to stop and ask a person
Step 5
Add guardrails
Least privilege, approval for risky actions, time and cost limits
Step 6
Evaluate & iterate
Test on real cases, read the transcripts, fix failures, repeat
Start simple: one agent, a few tools. Add more agents only when one clearly isn’t enough.
Continuous Calibration / Continuous Development
CC/CD: build small, then calibrate
Start low
Low agency, high human control
Deploy, then calibrate
Evaluate real use, fix errors
Earn autonomy
Add agency as trust grows
Source: Aishwarya Reganti & Kiriti Badam, “Why your AI product needs a different development lifecycle,” Lenny’s Newsletter. Diagram via LinkedIn Learning.

10 · Summary
Three things to remember
1
An agent is a model, tools and a loop.
It plans, acts, checks the result and adjusts until the goal is met.
2
Use agents for varied, checkable, tool-driven work.
If the steps never change, a script is cheaper. If mistakes are costly, keep a human in charge.
3
Build small, measure, then add autonomy.
Loop like CC/CD: start with low autonomy, evaluate, fix, and widen it as trust grows.
